transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-08
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Gupta (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (SentryLane Head of Platform), Rosa Martinez (SecOps), Evan Liu (Cloud Architect)

Summary: discovery focused on VPC orchestration, CIDR/IP planning, transit gateway vs peering strategy, private endpoints, egress and region constraints (EU + APAC). Customer has compliance constraints and wants to avoid CIDR overlap across multiple accounts; asking about cross-account attachments, PrivateLink vs Private Endpoint nomenclature, and how Redwood handles KMS, audit logs and data residency.

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro—i'm alex from redwood, ae — maya is our systems engineer who will walk through the deep bits. how are you folks doing?
[00:12] Daniel Park: good thanks. we pulled together the platform and security folks — ros a, evan, hi. we want to make sure the networking is nailed before we talk pricing or pilot.
[00:20] Rosa Martinez: hi all, yup security and compliance are primary for us, SOC2, encryption at rest, KMS integration, plus strict egress controls out of eu-west.
[00:28] Maya Gupta: thanks rosa, that's helpful. just to frame — redwood offers hosted, dedicated reserved pools, and private (vpc/on-prem). today's call is to understand your current vpc layout, any CIDR constraints, cross-account peering, and regional gating.
[00:40] Evan Liu: yeah, we run multi-account aws with a transit gateway. each business unit has own vpc ranges — sort of 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/16 variations. worried about overlap and routing table growth if we do lots of peering.
[00:53] Alex Chen: perfect — that maps to common patterns. quick question: do you manage IPs centrally (IPAM) or is it ad-hoc?
[00:59] Evan Liu: we're rolling out an IPAM but not fully enforced. right now we still have a few overlaps we need to clean.
[01:05] Maya Gupta: okay, two high-level approaches for private: 1) cross-account attachments via transit gateway where redwood's private deployment attaches as an account role and we peer via TGW; 2) native VPC peering or PrivateLink/private endpoints. TGW is simpler for many accounts but requires route table discipline.
[01:24] Daniel Park: what's the difference operationally? we already pay for a big transit gateway and have attachments for other services.
[01:29] Maya Gupta: with TGW you can attach redwood's dedicated VPC as another attachment — traffic stays on the aws backbone. advantages: single spoke, less peering sprawl, easier egress control. downsides: you need to accept routes, and if your CIDR overlaps with our allocated ranges we need to adjust — either via NAT or another subnet strategy.
[01:47] Rosa Martinez: can you do prefix translations or NAT for overlapping ranges? we hate touching customer routing tables.
[01:52] Maya Gupta: we can support a NAT/proxy layer in some configurations — e.g., a managed egress NAT in the redwood-managed account that translates to non-overlapping private ranges. that adds latency and complexity but is an option.
[02:05] Evan Liu: latency matters for inference — we can't add big NAT hops, it's doable for control plane but not ideal for real-time generation.
[02:12] Alex Chen: right — we typically recommend TGW attachments when low-latency SLOs are important. for high-performance use cases, Dedicated or Private with direct routing is preferred versus cross-account peering with extra hops.
[02:23] [Speaker 1]: (mumble) and also, what's the story for private DNS? if we put private endpoints in our vpc, will they resolve correctly?
[02:29] Maya Gupta: good question. we support conditional private hosted zones and split-horizon DNS for private endpoints. if you're using aws, we can create Route 53 private zones in the customer's account or support redwood-managed private zones with delegation. there are tradeoffs—delegation is simpler operationally for us but some customers prefer zones in their account for full control.
[02:48] Daniel Park: delegation might be okay provided we get audit logs and we can rotate keys. how does redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM?
[02:56] Maya Gupta: we integrate with customer-managed KMS for optional envelope encryption on sensitive artifacts. for private deployments you can bring-your-own-kms key and we can be configured to use it for model cache encryption and snapshot encryption. note: in hosted mode we manage KMS keys.
[03:12] Rosa Martinez: and for compliance we need full audit trail for data access across the inference plane. logs must be shipable to our SIEM.
[03:19] Alex Chen: we provide audit logs, per-request trace IDs, and you can configure log forwarding to your S3 / SIEM via our audit export connectors. will share SOC2 + logging docs after.
[03:31] Evan Liu: now the region question: we need inference to run in eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1 for EU and APAC latency. can you host in multiple regions and what about cross-region peering?
[03:42] Maya Gupta: yes, Redwood Private supports regional deployments. two options: 1) deploy regional clusters and route requests to the region based on geography; 2) centralize in one region behind a network path—less ideal for latency. For cross-region we either do TGW peering (aws-provided) or utilize private link equivalents. cross-region TGW attachments are supported but you must check inter-region data transfer costs and regulatory path for data residency.
[04:05] Daniel Park: data residency — EU data must stay in eu-west unless we have explicit encryption and contractual controls.
[04:10] Alex Chen: agreed. we offer region pinning and can commit to no-eu-egress for certain workloads with contractual controls. we'll include that in the checklist.
[04:18] [00:04:20] Rosa Martinez: about ip allowlists — we prefer to restrict source ip to specific ranges. if redwood is attaching into our TGW, how do we maintain allowlist stability? we're worried about churn.
[04:29] Maya Gupta: we publish stable egress IP ranges for Private deployments when requested, but for TGW attachments it's usually a stable attachment route. we can also support static Elastic IPs on NAT gateways for predictable egress. for dedicated hosted endpoints, egress ranges are documented per region.
[04:45] Evan Liu: would we need to open ports inbound? typically our security posture is deny-by-default.
[04:50] Maya Gupta: inbound is usually only from your subnets to our private endpoints — no public internet ingress. you'd have to allow the peered prefixes in your security groups. we can automate security group setup if you provide Terraform/state.
[05:03] Daniel Park: terraform — we operate everything as IaC. if we accept a TGW attachment, can we do the attachment via terraform provider or do you require a manual AWS console step?
[05:12] Maya Gupta: we provide terraform modules and can either provide a module that the customer imports or supply cloud-ops-assisted automation. for cross-account attachment we typically need an owner acceptance step in your account (a CloudFormation/Terraform apply with a role).
[05:25] [00:05:30] Alex Chen: quick digression — pricing flags. from network side, is transit gateway data transfer a big cost?
[05:31] Evan Liu: yes TGW inter-account charges and inter-region transfer can add up. we'll need an estimate.
[05:36] Alex Chen: we'll include egress estimates in the pricing sheet — both direct egress and TGW transfer.
[05:41] Rosa Martinez: security question — do you support SSO and SCIM for RBAC? the product owners want per-team tokens.
[05:48] Maya Gupta: yes SSO via SAML/OIDC and SCIM provisioning. for private deployments we integrate into your IdP and you control roles; for hosted we offer enterprise SSO.
[05:56] Evan Liu: what about audit/forensics? if we have a breach we need raw logs for investigations.
[06:01] Maya Gupta: audit logs are exportable; we can push to your S3 bucket, or stream to a SIEM via Kinesis/Logstash.
[06:08] Daniel Park: okay let's get into the nitty-gritty — our current VPCs are: 10.0.0.0/16 (platform-prod), 10.1.0.0/16 (platform-stage), 172.16.0.0/16 (infra), and we have some legacy 192.168 ranges. we want to avoid changing those.
[06:24] Alex Chen: thanks — we should run a compatibility check. two main patterns: 1) we ask you to reserve /24s for redwood in each account (non-overlapping) — that requires space in your IP plan; 2) we NAT/translate traffic on our side to non-overlapping ranges. the first is preferred for latency and simplicity.
[06:43] Evan Liu: reserving /24s might be tight, we only have a handful of /16s. can you work with smaller subnets?
[06:49] Maya Gupta: yes we can work with /28 -> /24 ranges depending on connection type, but need predictability. we'll send recommended sizes in the checklist.
[06:58] [00:07:00] Rosa Martinez: if redwood wants Route 53 delegation, how does that affect our DNS operations and internal resolvers? we use a private resolvers overlay.
[07:07] Maya Gupta: delegation is standard — we either create private zones in your account or we provide zone delegation to our private zones. you keep control and can audit changes. we also support IPAM-integrated DNS entries if you use AWS IPAM.
[07:20] Daniel Park: can the redwood deployment be air-gapped on-prem? we have a sensitive workload that can't leave our colo.
[07:26] Maya Gupta: yes — we offer an on-prem package for air-gapped deployments. that is heavier lift but is an option.
[07:33] Evan Liu: would that have the same orchestration interface as hosted?
[07:36] Maya Gupta: yes same API surface and console; just private control plane in your network. updates are coordinated with our release team.
[07:42] [00:07:45] Alex Chen: let's talk failover — if eu is down, can traffic fail over to apac or us? do you want automatic fallback?
[07:52] Daniel Park: not for the eu data — we need eu-only for some models. for others we can failover. but we'd like controls at the route level.
[08:01] Maya Gupta: you can set per-route region policies and model pinning. we recommend separate config for eu-restricted workloads. fallback policies can be automatic or manual; we can tag requests as eu-only.
[08:12] Evan Liu: and latency SLOs — what's the extra latency when going through TGW vs direct private endpoint?
[08:18] Maya Gupta: usually sub-ms inside region; but depends on topology. NAT or proxy adds 5-15ms typically. inter-region adds network propagation. we'll run a perf test once we have an attachment.
[08:29] [00:08:30] Rosa Martinez: are there any managed connectors to our private ca/secret store for cert rotation? we use HashiCorp Vault and our own PKI.
[08:39] Maya Gupta: we integrate with Vault for secrets and with your PKI via cert rotation APIs. we'll share the integration doc.
[08:45] Daniel Park: operational runbook — if something breaks who owns the fix for TGW route flaps?
[08:51] Alex Chen: typically severity 1 — network connectivity — we coordinate cross-team. for private deployments we have a joint runbook; for hosted, our infra handles the endpoint side but you'll manage your network. we'll include an escalation matrix.
[09:02] Evan Liu: okay, sounds reasonable. one more question: do you support egress IP allowlisting per customer in multi-tenant hosted? we want per-tenant IP ranges.
[09:11] Maya Gupta: for hosted we provide customer-level egress ranges on request; for dedicated/private it's naturally isolated and you get your own ranges.
[09:18] [00:09:25] Daniel Park: now on timelines — we aim to run a short pilot in jan, full rollout q2. security gating will be the main blocker.
[09:32] Alex Chen: great. we'll aim to get SOC2, private deployment checklist, and terraform examples over to you this week.
[09:39] Rosa Martinez: please include proof of pen testing and references for enterprise customers.
[09:44] Alex Chen: will do.
[09:46] Evan Liu: one tiny nit — what's the model of billing for private? is it license plus infra? or usage only?
[09:53] Alex Chen: typically for private we do platform fee + infra cost estimate; Dedicated has reserved capacity pricing. we'll include both with egress estimates.
[09:59] [00:10:00] Maya Gupta: action item recap — evan, please share CIDR map and account IDs. we'll run the compatibility check. alex will send checklist and pricing. i'll produce TGW attachment terraform and a sample architecture diagram.
[10:16] Daniel Park: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:19] Alex Chen: thanks all — we'll follow up by email with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the tech deep-dive.

Post-call notes (auto):
- Customer constraints: strict EU data residency, multi-account IP overlap, transit gateway in use, requires SSO/SCIM and KMS integration.
- Recommended immediate steps: run CIDR compatibility check; evaluate TGW attachment vs PrivateLink for low-latency; prepare egress cost estimates.
- References mentioned: SOC2 report, Terraform modules, TGW attachment sample, private deployment checklist (links to be sent).

Transcript end.
